{"id": "W4220754707", "doi": "10.1056/nejmoa2115869", "title": "Effect of Early Treatment with Ivermectin among Patients with Covid-19", "abstract": "BACKGROUND: The efficacy of ivermectin in preventing hospitalization or extended observation in an emergency setting among outpatients with acutely symptomatic coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19), the disease caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), is unclear. METHODS: We conducted a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, adaptive platform trial involving symptomatic SARS-CoV-2-positive adults recruited from 12 public health clinics in Brazil. Patients who had had symptoms of Covid-19 for up to 7 days and had at least one risk factor for disease progression were randomly assigned to receive ivermectin (400 μg per kilogram of body weight) once daily for 3 days or placebo. (The trial also involved other interventions that are not reported here.) The primary composite outcome was hospitalization due to Covid-19 within 28 days after randomization or an emergency department visit due to clinical worsening of Covid-19 (defined as the participant remaining under observation for >6 hours) within 28 days after randomization. RESULTS: A total of 3515 patients were randomly assigned to receive ivermectin (679 patients), placebo (679), or another intervention (2157). Overall, 100 patients (14.7%) in the ivermectin group had a primary-outcome event, as compared with 111 (16.3%) in the placebo group (relative risk, 0.90; 95% Bayesian credible interval, 0.70 to 1.16). Of the 211 primary-outcome events, 171 (81.0%) were hospital admissions. Findings were similar to the primary analysis in a modified intention-to-treat analysis that included only patients who received at least one dose of ivermectin or placebo (relative risk, 0.89; 95% Bayesian credible interval, 0.69 to 1.15) and in a per-protocol analysis that included only patients who reported 100% adherence to the assigned regimen (relative risk, 0.94; 95% Bayesian credible interval, 0.67 to 1.35). There were no significant effects of ivermectin use on secondary outcomes or adverse events. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with ivermectin did not result in a lower incidence of medical admission to a hospital due to progression of Covid-19 or of prolonged emergency department observation among outpatients with an early diagnosis of Covid-19. {"id": "W4307043809", "doi": "10.1001/jama.2022.18590", "title": "Effect of Ivermectin vs Placebo on Time to Sustained Recovery in Outpatients With Mild to Moderate COVID-19: A Randomized Clinical Trial", "abstract": "IMPORTANCE: The effectiveness of ivermectin to shorten symptom duration or prevent hospitalization among outpatients in the US with mild to moderate symptomatic COVID-19 is unknown. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of ivermectin, 400 μg/kg, daily for 3 days compared with placebo for the treatment of early mild to moderate COVID-19. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: ACTIV-6, an ongoing, decentralized, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled platform trial, was designed to evaluate repurposed therapies in outpatients with mild to moderate COVID-19. A total of 1591 participants aged 30 years and older with confirmed COVID-19, experiencing 2 or more symptoms of acute infection for 7 days or less, were enrolled from June 23, 2021, through February 4, 2022, with follow-up data through May 31, 2022, at 93 sites in the US. INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomized to receive ivermectin, 400 μg/kg (n = 817), daily for 3 days or placebo (n = 774). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Time to sustained recovery, defined as at least 3 consecutive days without symptoms. There were 7 secondary outcomes, including a composite of hospitalization or death by day 28. RESULTS: Among 1800 participants who were randomized (mean [SD] age, 48 [12] years; 932 women [58.6%]; 753 [47.3%] reported receiving at least 2 doses of a SARS-CoV-2 vaccine), 1591 completed the trial. The hazard ratio (HR) for improvement in time to recovery was 1.07 (95% credible interval [CrI], 0.96-1.17; posterior P value [HR >1] = .91). The median time to recovery was 12 days (IQR, 11-13) in the ivermectin group and 13 days (IQR, 12-14) in the placebo group. There were 10 hospitalizations or deaths in the ivermectin group and 9 in the placebo group (1.2% vs 1.2%; HR, 1.1 [95% CrI, 0.4-2.6]). The most common serious adverse events were COVID-19 pneumonia (ivermectin [n = 5]; placebo [n = 7]) and venous thromboembolism (ivermectin [n = 1]; placebo [n = 5]). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among outpatients with mild to moderate COVID-19, treatment with ivermectin, compared with placebo, did not significantly improve time to recovery. These findings do not support the use of ivermectin in patients with mild to moderate COVID-19. The molecular hypothesis of ivermectin's antiviral mode of action suggests an inhibitory effect on severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) replication in early stages of infection. Currently, evidence on ivermectin for prevention of SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 treatment is conflicting. OBJECTIVES: To assess the efficacy and safety of ivermectin plus standard of care compared to standard of care plus/minus placebo, or any other proven intervention for people with COVID-19 receiving treatment as inpatients or outpatients, and for prevention of an infection with SARS-CoV-2 (postexposure prophylaxis). {"id": "W3135420706", "doi": "10.1001/jama.2021.3071", "title": "Effect of Ivermectin on Time to Resolution of Symptoms Among Adults With Mild COVID-19: A Randomized Clinical Trial", "abstract": "IMPORTANCE: Ivermectin is widely prescribed as a potential treatment for COVID-19 despite uncertainty about its clinical benefit. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether ivermectin is an efficacious treatment for mild COVID-19. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Double-blind, randomized trial conducted at a single site in Cali, Colombia. Potential study participants were identified by simple random sampling from the state's health department electronic database of patients with symptomatic, laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 during the study period. A total of 476 adult patients with mild disease and symptoms for 7 days or fewer (at home or hospitalized) were enrolled between July 15 and November 30, 2020, and followed up through December 21, 2020. INTERVENTION: Patients were randomized to receive ivermectin, 300 μg/kg of body weight per day for 5 days (n = 200) or placebo (n = 200). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Primary outcome was time to resolution of symptoms within a 21-day follow-up period. Solicited adverse events and serious adverse events were also collected. RESULTS: Among 400 patients who were randomized in the primary analysis population (median age, 37 years [interquartile range {IQR}, 29-48]; 231 women [58%]), 398 (99.5%) completed the trial. The median time to resolution of symptoms was 10 days (IQR, 9-13) in the ivermectin group compared with 12 days (IQR, 9-13) in the placebo group (hazard ratio for resolution of symptoms, 1.07 [95% CI, 0.87 to 1.32]; P = .53 by log-rank test). By day 21, 82% in the ivermectin group and 79% in the placebo group had resolved symptoms. The most common solicited adverse event was headache, reported by 104 patients (52%) given ivermectin and 111 (56%) who received placebo. The most common serious adverse event was multiorgan failure, occurring in 4 patients (2 in each group). CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: Among adults with mild COVID-19, a 5-day course of ivermectin, compared with placebo, did not significantly improve the time to resolution of symptoms. The findings do not support the use of ivermectin for treatment of mild COVID-19, although larger trials may be needed to understand the effects of ivermectin on other clinically relevant outcomes. {"id": "W4212973150", "doi": "10.1001/jamainternmed.2022.0189", "title": "Efficacy of Ivermectin Treatment on Disease Progression Among Adults With Mild to Moderate COVID-19 and Comorbidities: The I-TECH Randomized Clinical Trial", "abstract": "IMPORTANCE: Ivermectin, an inexpensive and widely available antiparasitic drug, is prescribed to treat COVID-19. Evidence-based data to recommend either for or against the use of ivermectin are needed. OBJECTIVE: To determine the efficacy of ivermectin in preventing progression to severe disease among high-risk patients with COVID-19. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: The Ivermectin Treatment Efficacy in COVID-19 High-Risk Patients (I-TECH) study was an open-label randomized clinical trial conducted at 20 public hospitals and a COVID-19 quarantine center in Malaysia between May 31 and October 25, 2021. Within the first week of patients' symptom onset, the study enrolled patients 50 years and older with laboratory-confirmed COVID-19, comorbidities, and mild to moderate disease. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either oral ivermectin, 0.4 mg/kg body weight daily for 5 days, plus standard of care (n = 241) or standard of care alone (n = 249). The standard of care consisted of symptomatic therapy and monitoring for signs of early deterioration based on clinical findings, laboratory test results, and chest imaging. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who progressed to severe disease, defined as the hypoxic stage requiring supplemental oxygen to maintain pulse oximetry oxygen saturation of 95% or higher. Secondary outcomes of the trial included the rates of mechanical ventilation, intensive care unit admission, 28-day in-hospital mortality, and adverse events. RESULTS: Among 490 patients included in the primary analysis (mean [SD] age, 62.5 [8.7] years; 267 women [54.5%]), 52 of 241 patients (21.6%) in the ivermectin group and 43 of 249 patients (17.3%) in the control group progressed to severe disease (relative risk [RR], 1.25; 95% CI, 0.87-1.80; P = .25). For all prespecified secondary outcomes, there were no significant differences between groups. Mechanical ventilation occurred in 4 (1.7%) vs 10 (4.0%) (RR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.13-1.30; P = .17), intensive care unit admission in 6 (2.4%) vs 8 (3.2%) (RR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.27-2.20; P = .79), and 28-day in-hospital death in 3 (1.2%) vs 10 (4.0%) (RR, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.09-1.11; P = .09). The most common adverse event reported was diarrhea (14 [5.8%] in the ivermectin group and 4 [1.6%] in the control group). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial of high-risk patients with mild to moderate COVID-19, ivermectin treatment during early illness did not prevent progression to severe disease. The study findings do not support the use of ivermectin for patients with COVID-19. {"id": "W4312115096", "doi": "10.1101/2022.12.15.22283488", "title": "Effect of Ivermectin 600 μg/kg for 6 days vs Placebo on Time to Sustained Recovery in Outpatients with Mild to Moderate COVID-19: A Randomized Clinical Trial", "abstract": "BACKGROUND: Whether ivermectin, with a maximum targeted dose of 600 μg/kg, shortens symptom duration or prevents hospitalization among outpatients with mild to moderate coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) remains unknown. Our objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of ivermectin, dosed at 600 μg/kg, daily for 6 days compared with placebo for the treatment of early mild to moderate COVID-19. METHODS: ACTIV-6, an ongoing, decentralized, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, platform trial, was designed to evaluate repurposed therapies in outpatients with mild to moderate COVID-19. A total of 1206 participants age ≥30 years with confirmed COVID-19, experiencing ≥2 symptoms of acute infection for ≤7 days, were enrolled from February 16, 2022, through July 22, 2022, with follow-up data through November 10, 2022, at 93 sites in the US. Participants were randomized to ivermectin, with a maximum targeted dose of 600 μg/kg (n=602), daily vs. placebo daily (n=604) for 6 days. The primary outcome was time to sustained recovery, defined as at least 3 consecutive days without symptoms. The 7 secondary outcomes included a composite of hospitalization, death, or urgent/emergent care utilization by day 28. RESULTS: Among 1206 randomized participants who received study medication or placebo, median (interquartile range) age was 48 (38-58) years; 713 (59%) were women; and 1008 (84%) reported ≥2 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine doses. Median time to recovery was 11 (11-12) days in the ivermectin group and 11 (11-12) days in the placebo group. The hazard ratio (HR) (95% credible interval [CrI], posterior probability of benefit) for improvement in time to recovery was 1.02 (0.92-1.13; P[HR>1]=0.68). In those receiving ivermectin, 34 (5.7%) were hospitalized, died, or had urgent or emergency care visits compared with 36 (6.0%) receiving placebo (HR 1.0, 0.6- 1.5; P[HR<1]=0.53). In the ivermectin group, 1 participant died and 4 were hospitalized (0.8%); 2 participants (0.3%) were hospitalized in the placebo group and there were no deaths. Adverse events were uncommon in both groups. CONCLUSIONS: Among outpatients with mild to moderate COVID-19, treatment with ivermectin, with a maximum targeted dose of 600 μg/kg daily for 6 days, compared with placebo did not improve time to recovery. These findings do not support the use of ivermectin in patients with mild to moderate COVID-19. {"id": "W3168908540", "doi": "10.1097/mjt.0000000000001402", "title": "Ivermectin for Prevention and Treatment of COVID-19 Infection: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Trial Sequential Analysis to Inform Clinical Guidelines", "abstract": "BACKGROUND: Repurposed medicines may have a role against the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The antiparasitic ivermectin, with antiviral and anti-inflammatory properties, has now been tested in numerous clinical trials. AREAS OF UNCERTAINTY: We assessed the efficacy of ivermectin treatment in reducing mortality, in secondary outcomes, and in chemoprophylaxis, among people with, or at high risk of, COVID-19 infection. DATA SOURCES: We searched bibliographic databases up to April 25, 2021. Two review authors sifted for studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Meta-analyses were conducted and certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach and additionally in trial sequential analyses for mortality. Twenty-four randomized controlled trials involving 3406 participants met review inclusion. We evaluated secondary outcomes in relationship to safety and other efficacy end points. CONCLUSION: Ivermectin had no significant effect on preventing hospitalization of patients with COVID-19. Patients who received ivermectin required invasive MVS earlier in their treatment. text:
**Ivermectin for COVID-19: what the randomized trials show**

## Bottom line
The large, well-run, pre-registered randomized trials consistently find that ivermectin does not improve clinically important outcomes in COVID-19. That holds for hospitalization, death, time to recovery and viral clearance. The early "positive" evidence came mostly from small, low-quality studies, and some of those were later retracted or are suspected of fraud. How this literature changed over time is a good case study for a research methods course.

## 1. Large, rigorous trials (the core of the evidence)

| Trial | Design / setting | n | Dose | Primary outcome | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TOGETHER** [W4220754707] | Double-blind, placebo-controlled platform trial; 12 clinics in Brazil; outpatients at high risk | 1,358 (ivermectin vs placebo) | 400 µg/kg × 3 days | Hospitalization or ED observation >6 h | 14.7% vs 16.3%; RR 0.90 (95% CrI 0.70–1.16). Per-protocol analysis gave the same result |
| **ACTIV-6 (400 µg/kg)** [W4307043809] | Double-blind, placebo-controlled; decentralized; 93 US sites | 1,591 | 400 µg/kg × 3 days | Time to sustained recovery | HR 1.07 (0.96–1.17); 1.2% vs 1.2% hospitalized or died |
| **ACTIV-6 (600 µg/kg)** [W4312115096] (preprint) | As above; 84% vaccinated | 1,206 | 600 µg/kg × 6 days | Time to sustained recovery | HR 1.02 (0.92–1.13); median 11 vs 11 days |
| **PRINCIPLE** [W4392303143] | Open-label platform trial; UK community | 2,157 ivermectin vs 3,256 usual care | 300–400 µg/kg × 3 days | Self-reported recovery; hospitalization/death | Recovery about 2 days faster (HR 1.15), but below the pre-set threshold for a meaningful effect (probability 0.19). No effect on hospitalization/death (OR 1.02) or 6–12-month outcomes |
| **I-TECH** [W4212973150] | Open-label; 20 hospitals in Malaysia; age ≥50 with comorbidities | 490 | 400 µg/kg × 5 days | Progression to severe disease | 21.6% vs 17.3%; RR 1.25 (0.87–1.80) |
| **López-Medina** [W3135420706] | Double-blind; Colombia; mild disease | 400 | 300 µg/kg × 5 days | Time to symptom resolution | HR 1.07 (0.87–1.32) |

**Smaller trials pointing the same way:**
- IVERCOR, Argentina, n=501: no effect on hospitalization (OR 0.65, 0.32–1.31) [W3173645873].
- Mirahmadizadeh et al., n=393: neither a single nor a double dose reduced hospitalization [W4283363264].
- CORVETTE-01, Japan: no difference in time to a negative PCR test (HR 0.96) [W4377292376].
- PLATCOV: even a high dose (600 µg/kg × 7 days) showed no measurable antiviral effect, and the ivermectin arm was stopped for futility. Viral clearance was 9.1% slower, CI −27% to +12% [W4321366419].
- COVID-OUT also found no benefit. The database only has a JAMA news summary of it [W4297261569], so look up the primary NEJM paper (Bramante et al., 2022) before you cite it.

**Safety:** across these trials, adverse events were generally similar between groups. I-TECH reported more diarrhea with ivermectin (5.8% vs 1.6%) [W4212973150].

## 2. Systematic reviews

- **Cochrane living review (2022)** [W4283205481] is the best synthesis to anchor your review. Its key methods choice was to include only *prospectively registered* RCTs, which removed 7 of the 14 trials from the earlier version. With 11 trials (3,409 participants):
  - **Outpatients:** ivermectin probably has little or no effect on 28-day mortality (RR 0.77, 0.47–1.25; moderate certainty) and no effect on quality of life (high certainty).
  - **Inpatients:** very low-certainty evidence; effects remain uncertain.
  - **Prevention:** no eligible evidence.
- **Earlier positive meta-analyses** show how bad inputs produce bad conclusions:
  - Bryant et al. (2021) reported a 62% mortality reduction (RR 0.38) at "moderate certainty" [W3168908540]. It pooled many small, early studies, including some later questioned or retracted; one of them, Pott-Junior, appears in its reference list [W3134585354].
  - Hill et al.'s OFID meta-analysis [W3121596699] was retracted [10.1093/ofid/ofac056]. Its author list includes Elgazzar, the author of a trial at the centre of fraud concerns.
- **Hill, Mirchandani & Pilkington (2022)** [W4206432189] re-ran the analysis grouped by risk of bias. The apparent survival benefit depended on poor-quality studies:
  - The potentially fraudulent trial alone gave RR 0.08.
  - Low-risk-of-bias studies together gave RR 0.96 (0.56–1.66).

## 3. Research-integrity problems to handle in your review
Several studies in this literature have been retracted or withdrawn. Some database records don't show this, so check each included study against Retraction Watch or the publisher:
- **Elgazzar et al.** preprint [W3110602237]: reported dramatic mortality reductions. My understanding is that Research Square withdrew it in 2021 after data-integrity concerns. The database record here does **not** flag this, so confirm it with the publisher before citing.
- **Pott-Junior et al.**, *Toxicology Reports* pilot trial [W3134585354]: retracted [10.1016/j.toxrep.2022.04.009].
- **Samaha et al.**, *Viruses* (Lebanon): retracted [10.3390/v13112154].
- **IRICT**, *Expert Rev Anti-infect Ther* [W4283838215]: retracted in 2024 [10.1080/14787210.2024.2362097]. This trial had reported *harm* (HR 9.8 for death), so retractions cut both ways.
- **Hill et al. OFID meta-analysis:** retracted [10.1093/ofid/ofac056].

## 4. Suggestions for your methods
1. **Eligibility:** consider following Cochrane and requiring prospective registration, then run a sensitivity analysis with and without that rule.
2. **Risk of bias:** use RoB 2 and stratify results by risk-of-bias level, as Hill 2022 did.
3. **Integrity screening:** add a step that checks every included study for retractions, expressions of concern and implausible data.
4. **Separate the populations:** analyze outpatients, inpatients and prophylaxis separately; the evidence differs in certainty.
5. **Be careful with the PRINCIPLE result:** a statistically significant but clinically trivial effect in an open-label trial with self-reported outcomes is useful for teaching about blinding and minimal clinically important differences.

**A gap you should fill:** this search covered treatment trials. If prophylaxis is in scope, you'll need a separate search; one prophylaxis meta-analysis appeared in the results [W4313209660] but I didn't assess it. Also search the trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN) for completed trials whose results were never published, to check for publication bias.

I should have given you my criteria. Only randomized controlled trials of oral or intravenous ivermectin in people with confirmed or suspected COVID-19, compared with placebo, no treatment, standard care or another drug. No prophylaxis trials in people without COVID-19, no observational studies, no lab or animal studies, and no reviews. Please give me the full updated list of included trials.

{"id": "W4313121933", "doi": "10.3947/ic.2022.0127", "title": "An Open Label Randomized Controlled Trial of Ivermectin Plus Favipiravir-Based Standard of Care versus Favipiravir-Based Standard of Care for Treatment of Moderate COVID-19 in Thailand", "abstract": "BACKGROUND: The role of ivermectin in the treatment of moderate coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is controversial. We performed an open label randomized controlled trial to evaluate the role of ivermectin plus favipiravir-based standard of care versus favipiravir-based standard of care for the treatment of moderate COVID-19 infection. MATERIALS AND METHODS: An open-label randomized control trial was performed at Thammasat Field Hospital and Thammasat University Hospital from October 1st, 2021 to May 31st, 2022. Patients with moderate COVID-19 infections were randomized to the intervention (ivermectin plus favipiravir-based standard of care) or control group (favipiravir-based standard of care alone). Patients were followed up to 21 days. The primary outcome was the improvement in World Health Organization (WHO) category ordinal scale by 2 points. Secondary outcomes included duration of illness, development of severe COVID-19, and adverse reactions. RESULTS: There were 157 patients in the intervention and 160 patients in the control group. Characteristics, underlying diseases, and risk factors for severe COVID-19 were comparable in both groups. Improvement in the WHO-category ordinal scale by 2 points was achieved in 98.7% of the intervention group and in 99.4% of the control group (relative risk [RR]: 0.487; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.044-5.430). The median illness duration was 5.0 days (range, 3 - 28 days) in intervention group versus 5.2 days (range, 3 - 28 days) in control group (P = 0.630). Severe COVID-19 that required intensive care occurred in 2 patients (1.3%) in the intervention group and 1 patient (0.6%) in the control group (RR: 2.052; 95% CI: 0.184 - 22.857). No significant difference in serious drug adverse events was seen. CONCLUSION: In this study ivermectin plus standard of care was not associated with improvement in the WHO-category ordinal scale, reduced illness duration, or development of severe COVID-19 in moderately ill COVID-19 patients. Since the publication of the potential use of ivermectin as a treatment against the disease, a pleiad of information about it has been published. However, the evidence is not strong or weak enough to conclude its usefulness in the clinical evolution of patients infected with SARS-CoV-2. We evaluate the efficacy and safety of ivermectin in the treatment of Mexican patients with asymptomatic and mild COVID-19 in a three-day administration in comparison to placebo. METHODS: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was carried out in 66 adults with asymptomatic and mild COVID-19. Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 ratio to ivermectin plus acetaminophen or placebo plus acetaminophen. The primary endpoint was the proportion of subjects without a disease progression to severity according to COVID-19 guidelines by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) since randomization to 14 days. RESULTS: None of the participants presented progression to a severe state in either group. Viral load was measured on Days 1, 5, and 14. No significant differences were observed in baseline or 14-day between groups (p = 0.720 and 0.362, respectively). However, on Day 5, a significant difference in viral load was observed between groups (p = 0.039). The frequency of symptoms was similar between groups, and no significant differences were observed. The most frequent symptom was cough. One severe adverse event associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection was observed in the ivermectin group. CONCLUSIONS: At standard doses, ivermectin is not effective to prevent progression to a severe state or reducing symptoms in adults with asymptomatic and mild COVID-19. {"id": "W4393320918", "doi": "10.1016/j.jiph.2024.03.030", "title": "A randomized trial to assess the acceleration of viral clearance by the combination Favipiravir/Ivermectin/Niclosamide in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 adult patients (FINCOV)", "abstract": "BACKGROUND: The efficacy of the viral clearance and clinical outcomes of favipiravir (FPV) in outpatients being treated for coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is unclear. Ivermectin (IVM), niclosamide (NCL), and FPV demonstrated synergistic effects in vitro for exceed 78% inhibiting severe acute respiratory syndrome-coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) replication. METHODS: A phase 2, open-label, 1:1, randomized, controlled trial was conducted on Thai patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 who received either combination FPV/IVM/NCL therapy or FPV alone to assess the rate of viral clearance among individuals with mild-to-moderate COVID-19. RESULTS: Sixty non-high-risk comorbid patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 were randomized; 30 received FPV/IVM/NCL, and 30 received FPV alone. Mixed-effects multiple linear regression analysis of the cycle threshold value from SARS-CoV-2 PCR demonstrated no statistically significant differences in viral clearance rates between the combined FPV/IVM/NCL therapy group and the FPV-alone group. World Health Organization Clinical Progression scores and symptomatic improvement did not differ between arms on days 3, 6, and 10, and no adverse events were reported. No patients required hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, or supplemental oxygen or died within 28 days. C-reactive protein on day 3 was lower in the FPV/IVM/NCL group. CONCLUSION: Viral clearance rates did not differ significantly between the FPV/IVM/NCL combination therapy and FPV-alone groups of individuals with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, although the combined regimen demonstrated a synergistic effect in vitro. No discernible clinical benefit was observed. Further research is required to explore the potential benefits of FVP beyond its antiviral effects. {"id": "W4282964706", "doi": "10.3389/fmed.2022.919708", "title": "Non-effectiveness of Ivermectin on Inpatients and Outpatients With COVID-19; Results of Two Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trials", "abstract": "BACKGROUND: Ivermectin which was widely considered as a potential treatment for COVID-19, showed uncertain clinical benefit in many clinical trials. Performing large-scale clinical trials to evaluate the effectiveness of this drug in the midst of the pandemic, while difficult, has been urgently needed. METHODS: We performed two large multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials evaluating the effectiveness of ivermectin in treating inpatients and outpatients with COVID-19 infection. The intervention group received ivermectin, 0.4mg/kg of body weight per day for 3 days. In the control group, placebo tablets were used for 3 days. RESULTS: Data for 609 inpatients and 549 outpatients were analyzed. In hospitalized patients, complete recovery was significantly higher in the ivermectin group (37%) compared to placebo group (28%; RR, 1.32 [95% CI, 1.04-1.66]; p-value = 0.02). On the other hand, the length of hospital stay was significantly longer in the ivermectin group with a mean of 7.98 ± 4.4 days compared to the placebo receiving group with a mean of 7.16 ± 3.2 days (RR, 0.80 [95% CI, 0.15-1.45]; p-value = 0.02). In outpatients, the mean duration of fever was significantly shorter (2.02 ± 0.11 days) in the ivermectin group versus (2.41 ± 0.13 days) placebo group with p value = 0.020. On the day seventh of treatment, fever (p-value = 0.040), cough (p-value = 0.019), and weakness (p-value = 0.002) were significantly higher in the placebo group compared to the ivermectin group. Among all outpatients, 7% in ivermectin group and 5% in placebo group needed to be hospitalized (RR, 1.36 [95% CI, 0.65-2.84]; p-value = 0.41). Also, the result of RT-PCR on day five after treatment was negative for 26% of patients in the ivermectin group versus 32% in the placebo group (RR, 0.81 [95% CI, 0.60-1.09]; p-value = 0.16). CONCLUSION: Our data showed, ivermectin, compared with placebo, did not have a significant potential effect on clinical improvement, reduced admission in ICU, need for invasive ventilation, and death in hospitalized patients; likewise, no evidence was found to support the prescription of ivermectin on recovery, reduced hospitalization and increased negative RT-PCR assay for SARS-CoV-2 5 days after treatment in outpatients. Our findings do not support the use of ivermectin to treat mild to severe forms of COVID-19. {"id": "W3130646175", "doi": "10.1186/s12879-021-06104-9", "title": "Evaluation of the effectiveness and safety of adding ivermectin to treatment in severe COVID-19 patients", "abstract": "BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: An effective treatment option is not yet available for SARS-CoV2, which causes the COVID-19 pandemic and whose effects are felt more and more every day. Ivermectin is among the drugs whose effectiveness in treatment has been investigated. In this study; it was aimed to investigate the presence of gene mutations that alter ivermectin metabolism and cause toxic effects in patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia, and to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of ivermectin use in the treatment of patients without mutation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Patients with severe COVID19 pneumonia were included in the study, which was planned as a prospective, randomized, controlled, single-blind phase 3 study. Two groups, the study group and the control group, took part in the study. Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg/day for 5 days in the form of a solution prepared for enteral use added to the reference treatment protocol -hydroxychloroquine + favipiravir + azithromycin- of patients included in the study group. Patients in the control group were given only reference treatment with 3 other drugs without ivermectin. The presence of mutations was investigated by performing sequence analysis in the mdr1/abcab1 gene with the Sanger method in patients included in the study group according to randomization. Patients with mutations were excluded from the study and ivermectin treatment was not continued. Patients were followed for 5 days after treatment. At the end of the treatment and follow-up period, clinical response and changes in laboratory parameters were evaluated. RESULTS: A total of 66 patients, 36 in the study group and 30 in the control group were included in the study. Mutations affecting ivermectin metabolism was detected in genetic tests of six (16.7%) patients in the study group and they were excluded from the study. At the end of the 5-day follow-up period, the rate of clinical improvement was 73.3% (22/30) in the study group and was 53.3% (16/30) in the control group (p = 0.10). {"id": "W3162891398", "doi": "10.1177/03000605211013550", "title": "Ivermectin in combination with doxycycline for treating COVID-19 symptoms: a randomized trial", "abstract": "OBJECTIVE: We evaluated whether ivermectin combined with doxycycline reduced the clinical recovery time in adults with COVID-19 infection. METHODS: This was a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled trial in patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 symptoms randomly assigned to treatment (n = 200) and placebo (n = 200) groups. The primary outcome was duration from treatment to clinical recovery. Secondary outcomes were disease progression and persistent COVID-19 positivity by RT-PCR. RESULTS: Among 556 screened patients, 400 were enrolled and 363 completed follow-up. The mean patient age was 40 years, and 59% were men. The median recovery time was 7 (4-10, treatment group) and 9 (5-12, placebo group) days (hazard ratio, 0.73; 95% confidence interval, 0.60-0.90). The number of patients with a ≤7-day recovery was 61% (treatment group) and 44% (placebo groups) (hazard ratio, 0.06; 95% confidence interval, 0.04-0.09). The proportion of patients who remained RT-PCR positive on day 14 and whose disease did not progress was significantly lower in the treatment group than in the placebo group. CONCLUSIONS: Patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 infection treated with ivermectin plus doxycycline recovered earlier, were less likely to progress to more serious disease, and were more likely to be COVID-19 negative by RT-PCR on day 14. {"id": "W4292148078", "doi": "10.1056/nejmoa2201662", "title": "Randomized Trial of Metformin, Ivermectin, and Fluvoxamine for Covid-19", "abstract": "BACKGROUND: Early treatment to prevent severe coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) is an important component of the comprehensive response to the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) pandemic. METHODS: In this phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, we used a 2-by-3 factorial design to test the effectiveness of three repurposed drugs - metformin, ivermectin, and fluvoxamine - in preventing serious SARS-CoV-2 infection in nonhospitalized adults who had been enrolled within 3 days after a confirmed diagnosis of infection and less than 7 days after the onset of symptoms. The primary composite end point was hypoxemia (≤93% oxygen saturation on home oximetry), emergency department visit, hospitalization, or death. RESULTS: A total of 1431 patients underwent randomization; of these patients, 1323 were included in the primary analysis. METHODS: Proof-of-concept, pilot, randomized, controlled, outcome-assessor blinded trial to evaluate antiviral activity of high-dose IVM in 45 COVID-19 hospitalized patients randomized in a 2:1 ratio to standard of care plus oral IVM at 0·6 mg/kg/day for 5 days versus standard of care in 4 hospitals in Argentina. text:
I verified every included trial against its abstract only, not the full text. **34 trials met your criteria, plus one I couldn't classify.** Rezai et al. report two separate trials in one paper, so I counted them separately. The included trials are consistent: ivermectin does not reduce deaths, hospitalization or time to symptom resolution. The few positive results come almost entirely from small trials, and those mostly measured viral load or PCR results rather than how patients did.

## Included trials

**Outpatient / early treatment, ivermectin vs placebo or standard care**

| # | Trial | n | Design | Main findings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | López-Medina 2021, Colombia [W3135420706] | 400 | Double-blind (DB), placebo | Time to symptom resolution HR 1.07 (0.87–1.32); 10 vs 12 days, not significant |
| 2 | IVERCOR, Vallejos 2021, Argentina [W3173645873] | 501 | DB, placebo | Hospitalization 5.6% vs 8.4%, OR 0.65 (0.32–1.31) |
| 3 | TOGETHER, Reis 2022, Brazil [W4220754707] | 1,358 | DB, placebo | Hospitalization or long ED stay 14.7% vs 16.3%, RR 0.90 (0.70–1.16) |
| 4 | ACTIV-6 (400 µg/kg), Naggie 2022, USA [W4307043809] | 1,591 | DB, placebo | Recovery HR 1.07 (0.96–1.17); hospitalization/death 1.2% vs 1.2% |
| 5 | COVID-OUT, Bramante 2022, USA [W4292148078] | 1,323 analysed (whole trial) | DB, placebo; 2×3 factorial* | Primary composite aOR 1.05 (0.76–1.45); hospitalization/death aOR 0.73 (0.19–2.77) |
| 6 | Mirahmadizadeh 2022, Iran [W4283363264] | 393 | DB, placebo, 3 arms | Hospitalization not reduced by either single or double dose |
| 7 | Rezai 2022, outpatient trial, Iran [W4282964706] | 549 | DB, placebo | Hospitalization 7% vs 5%, RR 1.36 (0.65–2.84); fever about 0.4 days shorter |
| 8 | Angkasekwinai 2022, treatment cohort, Thailand [W4282595092] | 447 | DB, placebo** | No difference in oxygen desaturation, WHO score or symptom resolution (76% vs 82%); more blurred vision with ivermectin |
| 9 | Biber 2022, Israel [W4284890619] | 89 per-protocol | DB, placebo | More PCR-negative at day 6 (OR 2.62); fewer viable cultures; no clinical outcomes reported |
| 10 | COVER, Buonfrate 2022, Italy [W4212946211] | 93 | DB, placebo, high doses | No significant reduction in viral load |
| 11 | SAINT, Chaccour 2021, Spain [W3111068209] | 24 | DB, placebo | Day-7 PCR positivity unchanged (RR 0.92); faster recovery of smell |
| 12 | de la Rocha 2022, Mexico [W4311938754] | 66 | DB, placebo | No progression in either arm; symptoms similar |
| 13 | Chahla 2021, Argentina (preprint) [W3159407313] | 254 | Cluster-randomized, open | More outpatient discharges (98% vs 86%); uneven arm sizes and preprint only, so treat with caution |

**Hospitalized or mixed populations, ivermectin vs placebo or standard care (add-on designs included)**

| # | Trial | n | Main findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 | I-TECH, Lim 2022, Malaysia [W4212973150] | 490 | Progression to severe disease 21.6% vs 17.3%, RR 1.25 (0.87–1.80); deaths 3 vs 10 (RR 0.31, 0.09–1.11) |
| 15 | Rezai 2022, inpatient trial [W4282964706] | 609 | More complete recovery (37% vs 28%) but longer hospital stay; no effect on ICU, ventilation or death |
| 16 | Ahmed 2020, Bangladesh [W3107056972] | 72 (3 arms) | **Ivermectin-alone vs placebo comparison only** (the ivermectin + doxycycline arm is excluded): faster PCR clearance, 9.7 vs 12.7 days |
| 17 | Ravikirti 2021, India [W3182729893] | not stated in abstract | Day-6 PCR not different; discharge 100% vs 93% (p=0.045) |
| 18 | RIVET-COV, Mohan 2021, India [W3197929425] | 157 | PCR negativity and viral load not significantly different |
| 19 | Krolewiecki 2021, Argentina [W3170319714] | 45 | No difference in viral load overall; no clinical difference |
| 20 | Abd-Elsalam 2021, Egypt [W3164512669] | 164 | Deaths 3.7% vs 4.9%; ventilation 3.7% vs 3.7%; length of stay not significantly different |
| 21 | Shahbaznejad 2021, Iran [W3157727129] | 69 | Shorter dyspnea, cough and hospital stay (small trial) |
| 22 | Podder 2021, Bangladesh [W3150247726] | 62 | Recovery time and PCR not different |
| 23 | Saxena 2021, India [W3196420298] | not stated in abstract | Day-7 PCR positivity 34% vs 53%, not significant |
| 24 | Bukhari 2021, Pakistan (preprint) [W3126179459] | 86 | Faster viral clearance |
| 25 | Umar 2022, Pakistan [W4312323281] | 90 | Faster PCR negativity; difference in deaths/outcome not significant, though the authors claim benefit |
| 26 | Manomaipiboon 2022, Thailand [W4293176350] | 72 | PCR at day 7 and 14 not different; no secondary outcome differed |
| 27 | Sarojvisut 2022, Thailand [W4313121933] | 317 | Ivermectin + favipiravir-based care vs that care alone: no difference in WHO scale, illness duration or severe disease |
| 28 | Heydari 2022, Iran [W4405765493] | 107 (3 arms) | Ivermectin vs standard care: deaths 4.5% vs 11.8%, not significant; no outcome differed overall |
| 29 | Okumuş 2021, Turkey [W3130646175] | 66 | Ivermectin added to HCQ + favipiravir + azithromycin vs those drugs alone: improvement 73% vs 53% (p=0.10); deaths 20% vs 30% (p=0.37). Six patients were removed from the ivermectin arm only after randomization, which biases the comparison |
| 30 | Ochoa-Jaramillo 2022, Colombia [W4307216937] | 75 | ICU admission 21.6% vs 15.8%; deaths 5.4% vs 10.5%; none significant |

**Ivermectin vs another drug (head-to-head)**

| # | Trial | n | Main findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| 31 | Babalola 2021, Nigeria [W3129242298] | 62 | Ivermectin 6 mg or 12 mg vs lopinavir/ritonavir: faster PCR negativity with ivermectin |
| 32 | Niaee 2021, Iran [W3111064783] | 180 | Ivermectin arms vs HCQ arms: deaths 0–10% vs 17–20%. This is an outlier; check in the full text whether the ivermectin arms also got HCQ |
| 33 | Beltran-Gonzalez 2022, Mexico [W4220768079] | 106 | Ivermectin vs HCQ vs placebo: length of stay and deterioration/death not different (22% vs 24% vs placebo) |
| 34 | Galán 2021, Brazil [W3133698266] | 168 | Ivermectin vs chloroquine vs HCQ: deaths similar (21–23%) |

\*In COVID-OUT, metformin and fluvoxamine were assigned in a balanced way across the ivermectin and placebo groups, and the analyses adjusted for them. I think this meets your "same other treatments" rule, but you should decide.
\*\*Angkasekwinai randomized people with suspected COVID-19 before their PCR result. Only the PCR-positive treatment cohort is included.

**Couldn't classify:** El Sayed 2022 [W4283270938] compares ivermectin + colchicine with colchicine alone, which would be an eligible add-on comparison. The abstract says patients were "divided" into groups but never says they were randomized, so check the full text.

## Excluded, and why

- **Published after 2022:**
  - ACTIV-6 600 µg/kg: the journal article is from 2023 [W4321369786]. Your preprint rule points to the journal version, but the preprint [W4312115096] is from 2022, so decide which date applies.
  - PRINCIPLE [W4392303143], CORVETTE-01 [W4377292376], PLATCOV [W4321366419], Malektojari [W4319996285], Wijewickrema [W4400881102], Salama [W4406827333], FINCOV [W4393320918] and Exman [W4396610082].
- **Retracted or withdrawn:**
  - Elgazzar: the preprint was withdrawn [10.21203/rs.3.rs-100956/v4].
  - Samaha [10.3390/v13112154], Pott-Junior [10.1016/j.toxrep.2022.04.009] and IRICT [10.1080/14787210.2024.2362097].
- **Other treatments differ between arms:**
  - Mahmud, ivermectin + doxycycline vs placebo [W3162891398]. This is the largest positive trial, so leaving it out affects the conclusions.
  - Hashim [W4287129885], Chowdhury [W3133633583], Rahman [W3046318930] (randomization also not stated) and the ivermectin + doxycycline arm of Ahmed.
  - Babalola's Nigerian trial [W4243260355]: ivermectin was in both arms, so it doesn't test ivermectin.
- **Not randomized or observational:** Gorial [W3041503566], Carvallo [W3085858594], Sekhon [W4289979425] and Mahmood [W4403099903].
- **Not an original trial:** Sandhya Rani [W3213437465] reports exactly Ahmed et al.'s numbers.
- **Other route:** the nasal spray trial [W3168400794].
- **Prophylaxis:** Shoumann [W3129600723], the iota-carrageenan trials [W3143180683, W3100710042] and the Angkasekwinai prevention cohort.
- **Protocols only:** [W3139118535, W3118321049, W3033863786, W3182188484].
- **Preprints replaced by journal articles:** Biber [10.1101/2021.05.31.21258081], Ravikirti [10.1101/2021.01.05.21249310], ACTIV-6 [10.1101/2022.06.10.22276252, W4311753472] and de la Rocha [W6901825914].

## Synthesis

**Mortality.** Deaths were rare in the outpatient trials and showed no difference; ACTIV-6, for example, had 1.2% hospitalization or death in each arm. In hospitalized patients, most trials found similar mortality:
- Galán: 21–23% across arms
- Beltran-Gonzalez: 22% vs 24%
- Abd-Elsalam: 3.7% vs 4.9%
- Rezai's inpatient trial: no difference

Several small trials had point estimates favouring ivermectin, none statistically significant:
- I-TECH: RR 0.31 (0.09–1.11)
- Okumuş: 20% vs 30%
- Ochoa-Jaramillo: 5.4% vs 10.5%
- Heydari: 4.5% vs 11.8%

Niaee is the only trial reporting a large drop in deaths, and it compared ivermectin with HCQ. Overall, no trial shows a clear mortality benefit, and the wide confidence intervals mean small effects in either direction can't be ruled out.

**Hospitalization and disease progression.** The large, blinded trials found no effect:
- TOGETHER: RR 0.90 (0.70–1.16)
- COVID-OUT: aOR 0.73 for hospitalization/death, but 1.39 for ED visit, hospitalization or death
- IVERCOR: OR 0.65 (0.32–1.31)
- Rezai outpatients: RR 1.36
- Mirahmadizadeh: no difference
- I-TECH: progression to severe disease went the wrong way, RR 1.25

The estimates fall on both sides of no effect, which suggests there is no real effect.

**Symptom resolution.** The best evidence is null:
- López-Medina: HR 1.07 (0.87–1.32)
- ACTIV-6: HR 1.07 (0.96–1.17), median 12 vs 13 days
- Angkasekwinai: 76% vs 82% resolved
- Sarojvisut: 5.0 vs 5.2 days
- Podder: no difference

The few benefits are small or come from small, secondary analyses: shorter cough and dyspnea in Shahbaznejad (n=69), faster recovery of smell in SAINT (n=24) and about 0.4 days less fever in Rezai.

**Overall pattern.** Two things are worth discussing in your review:
- **Where the positive results sit.** They are concentrated in small, often open-label trials that measured lab results (PCR, viral load) rather than clinical outcomes: Babalola, Bukhari, Umar, Biber and Ahmed.
- **Large blinded trials are null.** The large, blinded trials measuring patient outcomes (TOGETHER, ACTIV-6, COVID-OUT, I-TECH, López-Medina) consistently show no benefit.

**Limits of this search:** it covered one database. I didn't search trial registries or non-English sources, and I screened abstracts only. Before you finalize, check the full texts of Niaee, El Sayed, Babalola and Chahla, and whether Chahla's and Bukhari's preprints were later published in journals.
Why didn't you include "Effectiveness of Ivermectin in SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 Patients"?

text:
You're right: it meets your criteria and should have been included. My mistake was a gap in the search, not a decision to exclude it.

## What the paper is
Chachar et al. 2020, *International Journal of Sciences*, Lahore, Pakistan [W3092176787]:
- **Design:** open-label randomized controlled trial, May–June 2020, in mild COVID-19.
- **Arms:** ivermectin plus symptomatic treatment (n=25) vs symptomatic treatment alone (n=25). This is an add-on design, so other treatments were the same in both arms.
- **Result:** at day 7, 64% vs 60% were asymptomatic (p=0.50), so no significant difference.
- **Other checks:** it's oral, published in 2020, and I found no retraction notice.

## Why I missed it
It didn't come up in any of my keyword searches. It was in the reference list of the Bryant meta-analysis, which I pulled in my first answer, but I didn't screen that list against your criteria. A systematic review should check the reference lists of earlier reviews, and I hadn't done that.

## What else that check turned up
I've now also screened the reference list of the Cochrane review [W4283205481]. It found a few more studies:

| Study | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Chachar 2020** [W3092176787] | **Include** | As above |
| **Kishoria 2020**, ivermectin added to HCQ vs HCQ alone, India [W3088905160] | **Include provisionally** | The title says open-label RCT and it's an add-on design. The abstract has no methods or results, so you'll need the full text |
| **Chahla 2022**, journal version [W4283385595] | **Replaces the Chahla 2021 preprint** [W3159407313] | Your rule is to use the journal article when both exist |
| Faisal 2021, ivermectin + azithromycin vs azithromycin, Pakistan [W3161928646] | **Unclear, leaning exclude** | It calls itself a "cross-sectional study" and allocated patients by "systematic random sampling", which is probably not true randomization |
| Spoorthi 2020, ivermectin + doxycycline [W3097342548] | Exclude | Randomization not stated, and the doxycycline isn't in the control arm |
| Camprubí 2020 [W3104739766] | Exclude | Retrospective |

**Chahla needs a closer look.** The journal version doesn't match the preprint:
- **Dosing:** 0.6 mg/kg in two doses, vs 24 mg weekly for 4 weeks in the preprint.
- **Diagnosis:** COVID-19 by physical exam "with negative RT-PCR", vs RT-PCR-positive in the preprint.
- **Design:** described simply as "randomized", vs "cluster-randomised" in the preprint.

The results are the same in both. Discrepancies like these are a research-integrity warning sign. I'd keep it in, but report a sensitivity analysis with and without it.

## Updated count
**36 trials included:** the 34 from before, plus Chachar and Kishoria (provisional), with Chahla's preprint swapped for its journal article. El Sayed and Faisal are still unclassified until you see the full texts.

**Effect on the synthesis:** none. Chachar found no difference in symptom resolution, the same null result as the higher-quality trials. Kishoria can't be assessed until you have the full text.

## Remaining gaps
I've only screened the reference lists of two reviews, Cochrane and Bryant. To be thorough, you should still:
1. Screen the reference lists of the other reviews from the first search, such as Popp/Cochrane updates, Roman et al. and Hill et al.
2. Check which papers cite the key trials, since that can surface later trials.
3. Search trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP, IRCT, CTRI) for completed trials and their linked publications.

Studies from small regional journals, like Chachar and Kishoria, are the most likely to be missed by keyword searches, so these steps matter.
List the papers you considered and excluded, with the reason for each.

These are all 140 records I screened and excluded (or haven't yet classified) across the searches and the two reference-list checks, grouped by reason. All decisions were made from abstracts. Where a record failed more than one criterion, it's listed under the main reason and the others are noted.

## A. Primary studies of ivermectin that I excluded (45 records)

**1. Retracted or withdrawn (4)**
- Elgazzar 2020, Research Square preprint [W3110602237]. The preprint was withdrawn [10.21203/rs.3.rs-100956/v4].
- Samaha 2021, *Viruses*, Lebanon [W3164155067]. Retracted [10.3390/v13112154].
- Pott-Junior 2021, *Toxicology Reports* pilot trial [W3134585354]. Retracted [10.1016/j.toxrep.2022.04.009].
- IRICT, Elshafie 2022, *Expert Rev Anti-infect Ther* [W4283838215]. Retracted [10.1080/14787210.2024.2362097].

**2. Other treatments not the same in both arms (6 records, plus one trial arm)**
- Mahmud 2021, ivermectin + doxycycline vs placebo [W3162891398]. The doxycycline wasn't in the control arm.
- Hashim 2021, Iraq, ivermectin + doxycycline vs standard care [W4287129885]. Same reason.
- Chowdhury 2021, ivermectin + doxycycline vs HCQ + azithromycin [W3133633583]. The combinations differ.
- Rahman 2020, Bangladesh, ivermectin + doxycycline vs HCQ + azithromycin [W3046318930]. The combinations differ, and randomization isn't stated.
- Spoorthi 2020, ivermectin + doxycycline [W3097342548]. Doxycycline wasn't in the control arm, and randomization isn't stated.
- Babalola 2021, Nigeria, ivermectin alone vs ivermectin + HCQ + azithromycin [W4243260355]. Ivermectin is in both arms, so the trial doesn't test ivermectin.
- Ahmed 2020, the ivermectin + doxycycline arm only [W3107056972]. The trial itself is included, using its ivermectin-alone vs placebo comparison.

**3. Published after 2022 (9 trials, 13 records)**
- ACTIV-6 600 µg/kg, journal article [W4321369786] (JAMA, February 2023). Its 2022 preprint [W4312115096] is set aside under your journal-version rule. You'll need to decide which date counts.
- PRINCIPLE [W4392303143] (2024).
- CORVETTE-01 [W4377292376] (2023).
- PLATCOV [W4321366419] (2023). Also excluded: its eLife editorial records [W4323320726, W4323344350, W4323344321].
- Malektojari [W4319996285] (2023).
- Wijewickrema, Sri Lanka [W4400881102] (2024).
- Salama, Ain Shams, journal article [W4406827333] (2024) and its conference version [W4393198428].
- FINCOV [W4393320918] (2024). Niclosamide was also given only in the intervention arm.
- Exman, losartan + ivermectin in cancer patients [W4396610082] (2024). Losartan was also given only in the intervention arm.

**4. Not randomized (12)**
- Gorial 2020 [W3041503566]: matched historical controls.
- Carvallo 2020 [W3085858594]: compared with published data.
- Rajter 2020 [W3091860795]: retrospective cohort.
- Bournigal, Dominican Republic [W3102430453]: retrospective.
- Camprubí 2020 [W3104739766]: retrospective.
- Safety-net hospital study [W3217293035]: prospective observational.
- Community hospitals cohort [W4386597728]: retrospective.
- Propensity-matched study [W4378516419]: retrospective.
- Abuja comparison [W4285014195]: consecutive cohorts.
- Sekhon 2022 [W4289979425]: observational cohort.
- Mahmood 2023 [W4403099903]: cross-sectional, no control group, and outside the date range.
- Case series of 100 patients [W3046413061].

**5. Prophylaxis in people without COVID-19 (10)**
- Shoumann 2021, household contacts [W3129600723].
- Chahla, ivermectin + iota-carrageenan in health workers [W3143180683]; Carvallo, topical ivermectin + iota-carrageenan [W3100710042].
- Prevention cohort of Angkasekwinai 2022 [W4282595092]. Its treatment cohort is included.
- Dhaka health workers [W3112738722], India health workers case-control [W3129541046], retrospective prophylaxis [W3136091706], Itajaí citywide [W4206412576] and ecological analysis [W4399761191]. These are also observational.
- HCQ/povidone-iodine prophylaxis [W3153015123]. Not an ivermectin trial.

**6. Wrong route (1)**
- Aref 2021, ivermectin nasal spray [W3168400794].

**7. Not an original trial (1)**
- Sandhya Rani 2021 [W3213437465]. It reproduces Ahmed et al.'s three-arm results exactly.

**8. Preprints and abstracts replaced by the journal article (6)**
- Biber preprint [10.1101/2021.05.31.21258081], replaced by [W4284890619].
- Ravikirti preprint [10.1101/2021.01.05.21249310], replaced by [W3182729893].
- ACTIV-6 400 µg/kg preprint [10.1101/2022.06.10.22276252] and conference abstract [W4311753472], replaced by [W4307043809].
- de la Rocha preprint [W6901825914], replaced by [W4311938754].
- Chahla preprint [W3159407313], replaced by [W4283385595].

## B. Not yet classified (2)
- El Sayed 2022, ivermectin + colchicine vs colchicine [W4283270938]. The abstract doesn't say patients were randomized, so check the full text.
- Faisal 2021, ivermectin + azithromycin vs azithromycin [W3161928646]. It calls itself "cross-sectional" and allocated patients by "systematic random sampling", which is probably not true randomization. I lean towards excluding it.

## C. Not primary studies (55)

**Protocols and design papers (7):** TOGETHER master protocol [W3182188484], SAINT protocol [W3033863786], SAINT-Peru [W3139118535], Iranian protocol [W3118321049], IVERCOR protocol [W3109673381], ACTIV-6 operations paper [W4388052115], and a statistical methods abstract [W4224247989].

**Systematic reviews and meta-analyses (25):**
- Cochrane [W4283205481] and Bryant [W3168908540], plus the OSF preprint of Bryant [W4254701078].
- Hill meta-analysis [W3121596699], since retracted [10.1093/ofid/ofac056], and Hill's bias analysis [W4206432189].
- [W3202911911, W4323305075, W3166599105, W3174188666, W4392649387, W3197310750, W4220763537, W3123539721, W3110533808, W4285545929, W4322712069, W4405274303, W3203491338, W4389885906, W4313209660, W4309361513, W3193087519, W3117652431, W4200397938]
- Protocol for a systematic review [W3200289841].

**Narrative reviews and book chapters (15):** [W3158596488, W4308623331, W4318041390, W4210315247, W4206186030, W4293769769, W4401965570, W7220516502, W4309818170, W3049611143, W3099512025, W4324130277, W3018040824, W4386686318, W4285096738]

**Commentary, news, letters and peer reviews (8):** [W3144228540, W4297261569, W4311448150, W4291378099, W4291378096, W3128164502, W3022811568, W4396553701]

## D. Lab, animal or computer-modelling studies (19)
- **Cell studies:** SARS-CoV-2 in vitro [W3014962324] and older antiviral studies [W1965936780, W2165157662].
- **Animal studies:** mouse [W3151682046], hamster [W4225660542, W3174079333] and zebrafish [W4288737360].
- **Computer modelling (docking and simulation):** [W3082948952, W3125444454, W3125207704, W3204740692, W3022875749, W3190401464]
- **Formulation:** inhalable ivermectin powder [W4285008448].
- **Hypothesis and mechanism papers:** [W3046117332, W3036124991, W3086865863, W3083341424, W4285005829]. The last one has also been retracted [10.3389/fmicb.2023.1216170].

## E. Off-topic search hits (19)
- **COVID-19 trials of other drugs (9):** sofosbuvir/daclatasvir [W3113301094], TOGETHER HCQ and lopinavir [W3156859932], TOGETHER fluvoxamine [W3208556307], ACTIV-6 fluvoxamine [W4306708170, W4315752560, W4386708327], HCQ outpatient trial [W3167819168], fluvoxamine + budesonide [W4366140579], remdesivir [W4200206478].
- **Other COVID-19 papers not about ivermectin's effect (5):** HCQ letter [W3137187469], fluvoxamine cost model [W4309163733], QT-risk review [W3081792974], fluvoxamine commentary [W4229055092], ivermectin politicisation news [W3144228540]. (The last is also counted under commentary in section C.)
- **Ivermectin outside COVID-19 (6):** malaria [W2606413115], onchocerciasis [W3120766993, W2773588431], high-dose safety [W2012188043, W3001552927], pharmacology reviews [W2296096754, W2104930292].

**Notes for your PRISMA flow diagram:**
- Category A is your "full-text assessed, excluded" list, with reasons. Categories C–E would normally be removed at title/abstract screening.
- I made every decision from abstracts only. The A and B decisions most likely to change on full-text review are the date-cutoff call for ACTIV-6 600, El Sayed and Faisal.
- Ahmed 2020 is included and excluded at once (one arm in, one out). Show this as a partial inclusion so it isn't double-counted.
